title: Gastrointestinal Neoplasms
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)

overview.intro: This chapter covers tumors of the digestive tract from the mouth and salivary glands to the anus, along with the liver, pancreas, and bile ducts. For each tumor it explains the precursor lesion and the molecular driver, why the tumor arises where it does, and how its growth and secretions produce the findings that appear in board questions: dysphagia, painless jaundice, refractory ulcers, flushing, anemia, or a palpable node. Most questions give a risk factor, a site, a marker, or a sign of spread and ask you to name the tumor or predict its behavior. If you can trace each finding back to anatomy, tumor biology, or a secreted product, you can reason through unfamiliar presentations.

sections.title: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma

blocks.text: The esophagus is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium until the gastroesophageal junction, and its two carcinomas follow from that lining. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) arises where carcinogens bathe squamous mucosa for years, so it favors the upper and middle thirds (the middle third most often). Adenocarcinoma needs glandular epithelium first, which reflux supplies by converting the distal squamous lining to intestinal-type columnar epithelium (Barrett esophagus); it therefore sits in the distal third and at the gastroesophageal junction.

For SCC, alcohol and tobacco act together, and very hot beverages, nitrosamines, and poor diet add risk. Anything that keeps irritants in contact with the mucosa or causes chronic injury raises risk: retained, fermenting food above an achalasic sphincter, a lye (caustic) stricture, and the iron deficiency, glossitis, and upper esophageal webs of Plummer-Vinson syndrome. TP53 mutation is common. SCC is the most common type worldwide, while adenocarcinoma predominates in the United States and other Western countries, driven by chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), obesity (raised intra-abdominal pressure promotes reflux), and smoking.

blocks.caption: Metaplasia is an adaptive change that becomes a precursor because the new epithelium keeps proliferating under injury.

blocks.text: Both types grow into the lumen and around the wall, so they cause mechanical dysphagia. A solid bolus needs a wide lumen, so dysphagia starts with solids (meat, bread) and progresses to liquids as the lumen narrows further. This contrasts with motility disorders such as achalasia, where solids and liquids are difficult from the start. Weight loss reflects both reduced intake and cancer cachexia driven by cytokines such as TNF and IL-6. Odynophagia, hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion, and cough from a tracheoesophageal fistula indicate local extension.

Most of the esophagus has adventitia instead of a serosa, and its submucosa has a rich longitudinal lymphatic network, so tumors spread early and often present late. Lymph node spread follows the level: cervical nodes for upper tumors, mediastinal and tracheobronchial nodes for middle tumors, and gastric and celiac nodes for distal tumors.

blocks.title: Esophageal carcinoma types
rows: Alcohol, tobacco, hot liquids, achalasia, caustic injury, Plummer-Vinson
blocks.caption: Both cause progressive dysphagia, solids then liquids, with weight loss.

sections.title: Gastric adenocarcinoma: intestinal and diffuse types

blocks.text: Gastric adenocarcinoma is the most common gastric malignancy. The Lauren classification divides it by how tumor cells hold together, and the two types differ in cause, appearance, and spread. Most cases present late with weight loss, early satiety, dyspepsia, and iron deficiency anemia from slow bleeding.
Intestinal type

Intestinal-type carcinoma forms glands that resemble colonic glands. It develops through a stepwise sequence of chronic gastritis, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma. Helicobacter pylori is the main driver: chronic inflammation generates reactive oxygen species and cell turnover, and atrophy lowers acid so bacteria colonize the stomach and convert dietary nitrates to N-nitroso compounds. Nitrosamines in smoked, salted, and pickled foods, low intake of fruit and vegetables, and autoimmune atrophic gastritis add risk. It typically forms an ulcerated or exophytic mass, often on the lesser curvature of the antrum, and is more common in older men.
Diffuse type

Diffuse-type carcinoma begins with loss of E-cadherin, the adhesion protein encoded by CDH1 (germline in hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, or acquired). Without it, cells detach and infiltrate the wall singly. Each cell fills with mucin that pushes the nucleus to the edge, giving the signet ring cell. The infiltrating cells provoke a desmoplastic reaction that thickens and stiffens the whole wall (linitis plastica, the leather-bottle stomach), so the stomach cannot distend and early satiety is prominent. It is not linked to intestinal metaplasia, affects younger patients, and has an equal sex distribution.

blocks.title: Intestinal versus diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma
blocks.caption: Classify by cell cohesion: glands mean intestinal type; single signet ring cells mean diffuse type.

blocks.text: Signs of spread

Abdominal lymph drains through the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct into the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins, so a hard left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) signals abdominal cancer. A periumbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) reflects peritoneal and lymphatic spread to the umbilicus. Bilateral ovarian metastases filled with mucin-rich signet ring cells form a Krukenberg tumor, classically from diffuse gastric cancer. Hematogenous spread goes first to the liver through the portal vein.

sections.title: Gastric MALT lymphoma and gastrointestinal stromal tumor

blocks.text: MALT lymphoma

The normal gastric mucosa has no organized lymphoid tissue. Chronic H. pylori infection recruits B and T cells and builds acquired mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) with lymphoid follicles. Within it, a B cell clone can expand into an extranodal marginal zone lymphoma, an indolent, low-grade B cell neoplasm. Its neoplastic cells are small to medium B cells (CD20 positive, CD5 negative, CD10 negative) that invade and destroy gastric glands, forming lymphoepithelial lesions.

Early tumor growth is antigen driven. The malignant B cells depend on help from H. pylori-specific T cells (CD40 ligand and cytokines that activate NF-kB), so early lesions regress when the bacterial antigen is removed. Tumors that acquire the translocation t(11;18)(q21;q21) produce an API2-MALT1 fusion protein that activates NF-kB on its own; they no longer need T cell help and do not regress. With further mutations, a MALT lymphoma can transform to diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor

A gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) is the most common mesenchymal tumor of the GI tract. It arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells within the muscularis propria that generate slow waves and express the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT (CD117). Most GISTs carry a gain-of-function KIT mutation, and a smaller group carries a PDGFRA mutation. The mutant receptor dimerizes and signals without its ligand (stem cell factor), driving continuous proliferation through the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways.

About 60% arise in the stomach and about 30% in the small intestine. Because the tumor grows within the muscle wall, it forms a well-circumscribed submucosal mass under intact or ulcerated mucosa; ulceration causes bleeding, and large masses cause fullness or obstruction. Histology shows spindle or epithelioid cells, and immunostaining for KIT (CD117) and DOG1 confirms the diagnosis. Malignant behavior is predicted by size, mitotic rate, and site, with gastric tumors behaving better than small bowel tumors of the same size.

blocks.caption: One is an immune cell tumor driven by antigen; the other is a pacemaker cell tumor driven by a mutant receptor.

blocks.text: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is the result of a gastrinoma, a neuroendocrine tumor that secretes gastrin without feedback control. Most arise in the duodenum, and fewer in the pancreas, within the region bounded by the junction of the cystic and common bile ducts, the second and third parts of the duodenum, and the junction of the neck and body of the pancreas. Many are malignant, and the liver is the main site of metastasis. About a quarter occur in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1, loss of the menin tumor suppressor), where they are often multiple and duodenal and accompany parathyroid hyperplasia and pituitary adenomas; hypercalcemia from the parathyroid component further stimulates gastrin release.

Normally, gastric acid in the antrum stimulates D cells to release somatostatin, which inhibits G cells, so gastrin falls as acid rises. Tumor cells lack this control. Gastrin also acts as a trophic hormone, causing parietal and enterochromaffin-like cell hyperplasia and thick gastric folds, so both the number of acid-producing cells and the signal to them rise.

blocks.title: Gastrinoma to ulcers and steatorrhea
steps: Gastrinoma secretes gastrin without acid feedback
Parietal cell hyperplasia; maximal acid secretion

Multiple, refractory ulcers, including distal duodenum and jejunum
Low intestinal pH inactivates lipase and precipitates bile acids
Fat malabsorption: diarrhea and steatorrhea
blocks.caption: Each manifestation follows from acid delivered where it is not normally neutralized.

blocks.text: The manifestations follow directly. Ulcers are multiple, recur, resist usual healing, and appear beyond the duodenal bulb (postbulbar duodenum or jejunum), a location ordinary peptic ulcers rarely reach. Diarrhea is common, may be the presenting symptom, and has two causes: the large volume of secreted acid overwhelms intestinal absorption, and acid irreversibly inactivates pancreatic lipase and precipitates conjugated bile acids, so micelles fail and fat is malabsorbed (steatorrhea).

Diagnosis rests on an inappropriately high gastrin in the presence of acid. A raised gastrin alone is not specific, because achlorhydria from atrophic gastritis and acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors also raise gastrin through loss of acid feedback; the gastric pH separates them. Secretin normally inhibits gastrin release from G cells, but gastrinoma cells express secretin receptors that stimulate release, so intravenous secretin produces a paradoxical rise in serum gastrin.

blocks.title: Worked example: two patients with high gastrin
blocks.text: Patient A has fasting gastrin 900 pg/mL (reference under about 100 pg/mL) and gastric pH 1.5; after secretin, gastrin rises to 1,150 pg/mL. Patient B has fasting gastrin 700 pg/mL, gastric pH 6.5, and vitamin B12 deficiency. Step 1: in B, high pH means no acid, so gastrin is high because feedback is absent; this fits autoimmune atrophic gastritis. Step 2: in A, gastrin is high despite strong acid, so secretion is autonomous. Step 3: the rise of about 250 pg/mL after secretin, which would normally lower gastrin, confirms a gastrinoma.

Carcinoid tumors are well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors arising from enterochromaffin cells of the gut epithelium. They stain for chromogranin A and synaptophysin and grow slowly. The small intestine, especially the ileum, is the most common site of carcinoids that metastasize and cause symptoms, while appendiceal carcinoids are often small, found incidentally, and rarely spread. Small bowel carcinoids may cause obstruction or intussusception, and their secretions provoke dense fibrosis of the mesentery that kinks the bowel.

Midgut carcinoids make serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) from tryptophan by tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, along with kallikrein (which generates bradykinin), tachykinins, and prostaglandins; histamine comes mainly from foregut (gastric and bronchial) carcinoids. Serotonin is inactivated by monoamine oxidase (MAO) to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), which is excreted in urine. A raised 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA is the classic marker. Heavy diversion of tryptophan to serotonin can leave too little for niacin synthesis, producing pellagra.

Only a minority of patients with carcinoid tumors develop carcinoid syndrome, and the reason is anatomical. Venous blood from a small bowel tumor enters the portal vein, and hepatic MAO inactivates serotonin before it reaches the systemic circulation. Once tumor deposits grow in the liver, their products enter the hepatic veins directly and reach the right heart. Carcinoids that drain outside the portal system, such as bronchial or ovarian tumors, can cause the syndrome without liver metastasis.

blocks.text: Other small intestinal tumors are uncommon relative to the size of the organ. Besides carcinoid, they include adenocarcinoma (most often duodenal and periampullary), lymphoma, and GIST.

blocks.predict: A patient with liver metastases from an ileal carcinoid has tricuspid regurgitation. Why are the mitral and aortic valves spared?
blocks.explain: Serotonin reaches the right heart through the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava, but pulmonary MAO inactivates it before blood reaches the left heart. A right-to-left shunt or a bronchial carcinoid can involve the left side.

blocks.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary malignancy of the liver. Most cases arise in a cirrhotic liver, where repeated cycles of hepatocyte necrosis and regeneration, chronic inflammation with reactive oxygen species, and telomere shortening accumulate mutations in a field of proliferating cells. The risk factors are therefore mainly causes of chronic liver injury, with two important exceptions in which a carcinogen acts directly on hepatocyte DNA.

blocks.title: Risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma
rows: DNA virus integrates into host DNA; HBx protein disrupts growth control and p53; can cause HCC without cirrhosis
RNA virus that does not integrate; acts through chronic inflammation and cirrhosis
Iron catalyzes free radical formation; fibrosis and cirrhosis
Hepatic activation to an epoxide that mutates TP53 codon 249
blocks.caption: HBV and aflatoxin act directly on DNA; most other risks work through cirrhosis.

blocks.text: Two exceptions deserve detail. Hepatitis B virus is a DNA virus whose genome integrates into hepatocyte chromosomes, causing insertional mutations and genomic instability, and its HBx protein transactivates host growth genes and binds p53. HBV can therefore produce HCC even without cirrhosis. Aflatoxin B1 comes from Aspergillus flavus growing on improperly stored grains and peanuts. Hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes convert it to aflatoxin B1-8,9-epoxide, which binds guanine and causes a G to T transversion at codon 249 of TP53 (arginine to serine). HBV and aflatoxin together multiply risk, which is why HCC is common in parts of sub-Saharan Africa and East Asia.

HCC may present as hepatomegaly, right upper quadrant pain, weight loss, and a liver mass, or as sudden decompensation of known cirrhosis with new ascites, encephalopathy, or variceal bleeding. Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), a fetal plasma protein that the tumor re-expresses, is raised in many patients (normal adult level under about 10 ng/mL); it is not specific, because it also rises in pregnancy, yolk sac tumors, and regenerating liver, and it is normal in a substantial minority of HCC.

HCC has a strong tendency to invade blood vessels. Growth into the portal vein causes portal vein thrombosis and worsens portal hypertension, invasion of the hepatic veins can produce Budd-Chiari syndrome, and hematogenous metastasis goes most often to the lungs. Paraneoplastic effects include erythrocytosis from erythropoietin and hypoglycemia. The fibrolamellar variant is an important exception: it affects adolescents and young adults without cirrhosis or viral hepatitis, shows tumor cells in lamellar bands of collagen, and usually has a normal AFP.

sections.title: Liver metastases, peritoneal tumors, and benign liver lesions

blocks.text: Metastases are far more common than primary tumors in both the liver and the peritoneum. The liver receives the whole portal venous drainage of the GI tract plus systemic arterial blood, and its sinusoids are lined by fenestrated endothelium without a continuous basement membrane, so circulating tumor cells lodge and reach hepatocytes easily. The usual primaries are colon, pancreas, stomach, breast, and lung, plus melanoma. Metastases typically form multiple nodules of different sizes; subcapsular nodules may show central necrosis and umbilication. Because a large reserve of normal liver remains, synthetic function is preserved until late, and the earliest laboratory change is often a raised alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase from local bile duct obstruction.

The peritoneum is seeded by transcoelomic spread, most often from ovarian, gastric, colorectal, and pancreatic carcinomas. Tumor implants on serosal surfaces and the omentum (an omental cake) leak protein and block lymphatic drainage, producing malignant ascites. Primary peritoneal tumors are rare and include malignant mesothelioma, associated with asbestos exposure, and primary peritoneal serous carcinoma. Mucinous neoplasms of the appendix can fill the peritoneal cavity with gelatinous mucin (pseudomyxoma peritonei).
Benign liver lesions

Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the liver. It consists of large, blood-filled vascular channels lined by a single layer of endothelium, is usually small, subcapsular, and asymptomatic, and is found incidentally on imaging. Its vascular nature means percutaneous needle biopsy risks serious bleeding.

Hepatocellular adenoma is a benign proliferation of hepatocytes that lacks portal tracts and bile ducts. It occurs mainly in young women using oral contraceptives and in anabolic steroid users, because estrogens and androgens stimulate hepatocyte growth, and in glycogen storage disease. The tumor is supplied by thin-walled arteries without a portal system, often lies beneath the capsule, and can rupture into the peritoneal cavity, causing sudden pain and hemorrhagic shock; risk is greatest in pregnancy, when estrogen and blood volume are high. Adenomas with activating beta-catenin mutations can transform into hepatocellular carcinoma.

sections.title: White oral lesions and oral and oropharyngeal carcinoma

blocks.text: Oral mucosa is stratified squamous epithelium that is moist and usually nonkeratinized. When it thickens, keratinizes, or is covered by a membrane, it looks white, so several unrelated processes share that appearance. The first bedside test is whether the white material scrapes off, because that separates a surface coating from a change within the epithelium itself.

blocks.caption: Leukoplakia is a clinical description, not a diagnosis; only histology shows whether dysplasia is present.

blocks.text: Leukoplakia is defined clinically as a white patch or plaque that cannot be scraped off and cannot be attributed to another disease. Histology ranges from simple hyperkeratosis to dysplasia or carcinoma in situ, and a proportion progresses to invasive cancer, so the lesion must be sampled. A red velvety patch (erythroplakia) is less common but much more often dysplastic. Hairy leukoplakia is a marker of immune suppression rather than a precursor of cancer.
Oral and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma

Most malignancies of the oral cavity are squamous cell carcinomas. Tobacco (smoked or chewed, including betel quid) and alcohol act synergistically: alcohol dissolves carcinogens and increases their penetration of the mucosa, and its metabolite acetaldehyde is itself mutagenic. Because the whole lining is exposed, many separate areas accumulate mutations (field cancerization), which explains multiple primary tumors and second primaries in the larynx, esophagus, and lung. TP53 mutation is common. Typical sites are the lateral tongue and floor of the mouth, and the lower lip is affected by ultraviolet exposure. Spread is to cervical lymph nodes.

Oropharyngeal carcinoma of the tonsils and base of tongue follows a different path. High-risk human papillomavirus, mainly HPV-16, infects the reticulated epithelium of the tonsillar crypts. Its E6 protein targets p53 for degradation and its E7 protein inactivates Rb, so TP53 is typically not mutated. Loss of Rb function leads to overexpression of p16, which serves as a surrogate marker. These tumors occur in younger patients, often nonsmokers, frequently present as a cystic neck node, and have a better prognosis than tobacco-related tumors.

Ductal adenocarcinoma accounts for about 85% of pancreatic cancers and is one of the most lethal cancers, because it is usually unresectable or metastatic at diagnosis. It arises from ductal epithelium through microscopic precursors called pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN). An activating KRAS mutation is found in over 90% of tumors and appears early; it locks the RAS GTPase in its active GTP-bound state and drives proliferation. Inactivation of CDKN2A (p16), then TP53 and SMAD4, follows as the lesion progresses. Smoking is the strongest environmental risk; chronic pancreatitis, long-standing diabetes, obesity, age, and inherited syndromes (BRCA2, hereditary pancreatitis, Peutz-Jeghers, Lynch) add risk. The tumor is gray-white and very hard because of intense desmoplasia, and it typically invades nerves, lymphatics, and the retroperitoneum early.
Location determines presentation. About 60% arise in the head, where the intrapancreatic common bile duct passes through the gland.

blocks.title: Pancreatic head tumor to Courvoisier sign
steps: Tumor in pancreatic head encases the distal common bile duct
Slow, progressive obstruction without inflammation
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia: jaundice, dark urine, pale stool, pruritus
Bile backs up into a previously healthy gallbladder

blocks.caption: Gradual obstruction of a normal duct system causes painless jaundice with a distended gallbladder.

blocks.text: Courvoisier sign, a palpable nontender gallbladder with jaundice, points to malignant obstruction of the distal common bile duct, classically a pancreatic head carcinoma. A gallstone in the common bile duct usually does not produce it, because repeated cholecystitis has made the gallbladder fibrotic and unable to distend. Tumors of the body and tail obstruct nothing early, so they present late with weight loss and deep epigastric pain radiating to the back, from invasion of the celiac nerve plexus.

Weight loss reflects cachexia plus maldigestion when the pancreatic duct is blocked. Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome), recurrent venous thromboses at changing sites, arises because tumor cells release mucins and tissue factor that activate coagulation. New-onset diabetes in an older adult can be an early sign. CA 19-9, a sialylated Lewis blood group antigen, is raised in most patients, but it is not specific (it rises in any biliary obstruction and in other cancers) and is absent in people who cannot synthesize Lewis antigens, so it is used to follow known disease rather than to screen.

blocks.predict: A jaundiced patient has a palpable, nontender gallbladder. Why does this argue against a common bile duct stone?
blocks.explain: Stone disease usually follows years of cholecystitis that leaves the gallbladder scarred and noncompliant, so it cannot distend. Slow malignant obstruction of a healthy system lets the gallbladder fill and stretch.
blocks.check: The flow figure and the paragraph on Courvoisier sign.

blocks.text: Colorectal adenocarcinoma is one of the most common causes of cancer death, with incidence rising steeply after about age 50. Most cases follow one of three molecular routes from a benign precursor to invasive cancer. The chromosomal instability (adenoma-carcinoma) pathway is the most common. The mismatch repair pathway underlies Lynch syndrome and some sporadic tumors: loss of MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2 lets replication errors accumulate in short repeated sequences (microsatellite instability). The serrated pathway, described with polyps, starts with BRAF mutation and promoter methylation.

blocks.title: Adenoma-carcinoma sequence
steps: Loss of APC in normal colonic mucosa
Beta-catenin accumulates and drives proliferation
Small adenoma forms
KRAS mutation enlarges the adenoma
Loss of TP53 (with other changes, often chromosome 18q)
Invasive adenocarcinoma through the muscularis mucosae
blocks.caption: APC normally targets beta-catenin for destruction; its loss is the first step in familial adenomatous polyposis and most sporadic tumors.

blocks.text: Hereditary syndromes show each pathway in its purest form. Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), from a germline APC mutation, produces hundreds to thousands of adenomas, and carcinoma develops in nearly all affected people by middle age. Lynch syndrome, from a germline mismatch repair gene mutation, produces few polyps but rapid progression, mainly in the right colon, with added endometrial, ovarian, and other cancers; both are autosomal dominant. Chronic inflammatory bowel disease (especially extensive, long-standing ulcerative colitis) raises risk through flat dysplasia in inflamed mucosa, with TP53 changes occurring early. Other risks include age, family history, diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, obesity, and smoking.

Symptoms depend on the side of the colon. The cecum and ascending colon have a wide lumen and liquid contents, so tumors grow as bulky exophytic masses and bleed slowly before they obstruct, producing iron deficiency anemia, fatigue, and weight loss. The descending and sigmoid colon is narrower and carries formed stool, so an annular tumor (napkin-ring, apple-core narrowing on imaging) causes a change in bowel habit, thin stools, visible blood, and obstruction. Rectal tumors add tenesmus and bright red bleeding. Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) bacteremia or endocarditis is associated with colonic neoplasia.

Mismatch repair and serrated tumors more common
blocks.caption: Right-sided tumors bleed silently; left-sided tumors obstruct.

blocks.text: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a glycoprotein expressed by many adenocarcinomas. It is not used to screen, because it is often normal in early cancer and is raised in smokers, inflammatory bowel disease, and other cancers. A raised preoperative CEA that falls after complete resection and then rises again indicates recurrence. Colorectal cancer spreads to regional nodes and through the portal vein to the liver, while low rectal tumors can drain into systemic veins and reach the lungs.

A polyp is any mass projecting into the lumen. It may be sessile (broad-based) or pedunculated (on a stalk), and its importance depends on whether its epithelium is neoplastic. Classification follows the cell biology.

Hyperplastic polyps are the most common non-neoplastic polyps. They are small (usually under 5 mm), found mainly in the rectosigmoid, and form because surface epithelial cells are shed more slowly and pile up, giving a serrated, saw-tooth outline confined to the upper crypts. They have negligible malignant potential.

Adenomas are neoplastic by definition, because their epithelium is dysplastic, with enlarged, elongated, hyperchromatic nuclei. They are the precursors of most colorectal cancer. They are classified by architecture: tubular adenomas (mostly tubular glands, the most common type), tubulovillous adenomas (mixed), and villous adenomas (long finger-like projections, usually sessile). Malignant risk rises with size (especially over about 1 cm), with the villous component, and with high-grade dysplasia, because each reflects more accumulated mutations. Large villous adenomas can secrete mucus rich in protein and potassium, causing hypokalemia.

Sessile serrated lesions look like hyperplastic polyps but are premalignant. They are flat, often in the right colon, and serration extends to the base of the crypts, which become dilated and spread sideways along the muscularis mucosae. They begin with a BRAF mutation and widespread CpG island methylation; methylation that silences MLH1 produces microsatellite instability. Because they are flat and pale, they are easily missed.

Hamartomatous polyps are disorganized overgrowths of tissue normally present at the site. Juvenile polyps occur in children, usually in the rectum, and contain cystically dilated glands in an inflamed lamina propria; they bleed or prolapse. A solitary juvenile polyp carries little risk, but juvenile polyposis syndrome (SMAD4 or BMPR1A) raises cancer risk. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (autosomal dominant, STK11) causes hamartomatous polyps with branching smooth muscle, mainly in the small intestine, where they can lead to intussusception, plus dark freckles on the lips and oral mucosa and a raised risk of GI, breast, pancreatic, and gonadal cancers.

blocks.predict: Two 6 mm serrated polyps are removed, one from the sigmoid with serration in the upper crypts and one from the cecum with dilated, sideways crypt bases. Which is a precursor of cancer?
blocks.explain: The cecal lesion is a sessile serrated lesion; its BRAF mutation and methylation, including MLH1 silencing, lead to carcinoma. The sigmoid lesion is a hyperplastic polyp from slowed cell shedding.

blocks.text: Most salivary gland tumors arise in the parotid gland, and most parotid tumors are benign. The proportion that is malignant rises as gland size falls, so a mass in the submandibular, sublingual, or a minor salivary gland is more likely to be malignant. A benign parotid tumor typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, mobile mass in front of or below the ear. Pain, rapid growth, fixation, or facial nerve weakness suggests malignancy, because the facial nerve runs through the parotid and infiltrating tumors invade it.

Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary gland tumor and is usually parotid. It is called a mixed tumor because it contains epithelial and myoepithelial cells in a chondromyxoid stroma that can resemble cartilage; myoepithelial cells are thought to produce the mesenchymal-appearing matrix. The tumor is only partly encapsulated, and small fingerlike projections extend through the capsule, so a lesion shelled out along its surface leaves tumor behind and recurs. Long-standing or recurrent tumors carry a small risk of malignant transformation (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma).

Warthin tumor (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum) is the second most common benign salivary tumor and occurs almost only in the parotid. It affects older adults and is strongly associated with smoking, and it is bilateral or multifocal in about 10% of cases. Histology is distinctive: cystic spaces lined by a double layer of oncocytic epithelial cells rest on a dense lymphoid stroma with germinal centers.

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common primary malignant salivary tumor and most often arises in the parotid. It is composed of mucus-secreting, squamous (epidermoid), and intermediate cells, and its behavior varies with grade. Many carry a CRTC1-MAML2 fusion gene from t(11;19). Adenoid cystic carcinoma, which often arises in minor salivary glands, is notable for perineural invasion that causes pain and allows recurrence along nerves.

sections.title: Biliary tract carcinomas and anal carcinoma

blocks.text: Cholangiocarcinoma

Cholangiocarcinoma is an adenocarcinoma of bile duct epithelium. It is classified by site as intrahepatic, perihilar (at the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts, the most common site), or distal. Its risk factors share chronic inflammation and bile stasis, which keep cholangiocytes proliferating under injury. Primary sclerosing cholangitis, a fibrosing disease of the bile ducts usually accompanying ulcerative colitis, is the main Western risk. In East and Southeast Asia, the liver flukes Clonorchis sinensis and Opisthorchis viverrini, acquired from raw freshwater fish, live in the ducts and cause chronic inflammation; choledochal cysts and hepatolithiasis add risk.

Most patients present with painless obstructive jaundice, pruritus, pale stools, dark urine, raised alkaline phosphatase, and weight loss. The gallbladder finding helps localize the block: a perihilar tumor lies above the cystic duct, so the gallbladder stays empty, while a distal tumor allows it to distend like a pancreatic head tumor. Adenocarcinoma of the ampulla of Vater obstructs early, so it presents with jaundice while still small; necrosis of the tumor can make jaundice fluctuate, and bleeding into the duodenum can cause occult blood loss and anemia.
Gallbladder adenocarcinoma

Gallbladder carcinoma is the most common malignancy of the extrahepatic biliary tract. Gallstones are present in most cases and are thought to act through chronic irritation and inflammation; a calcified (porcelain) gallbladder also signals risk. It affects older women more than men. Early disease causes no specific symptoms, and the thin wall lies against the liver, so it usually invades the liver or bile ducts before diagnosis; jaundice then signals advanced disease.
Anal carcinoma

The pectinate (dentate) line divides the anal canal by embryology. Above it, the lining is columnar (endoderm), drains to internal iliac nodes, and has visceral innervation, so tumors there are usually adenocarcinomas. Below it, the lining is stratified squamous (ectoderm), drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and has somatic pudendal innervation, so lesions there are painful. Anal squamous cell carcinoma arises at the transformation zone and below, and most cases are caused by high-risk HPV, mainly HPV-16, through the same E6 and E7 mechanism as in cervical cancer. Risk is highest with receptive anal intercourse and HIV or other immunosuppression; the precursor is anal intraepithelial neoplasia.

blocks.title: Worked example: locating painless jaundice
blocks.text: Three patients have painless conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with raised alkaline phosphatase. Patient A has a distended, nontender gallbladder; B has dilated intrahepatic ducts, a collapsed gallbladder, and long-standing ulcerative colitis; C has jaundice that waxes and wanes with occult blood in the stool. Step 1: a distended gallbladder means the block lies below the cystic duct, so A fits a pancreatic head or distal bile duct tumor. Step 2: in B the block lies above the cystic duct; with ulcerative colitis, suspect primary sclerosing cholangitis with perihilar cholangiocarcinoma. Step 3: in C, a small tumor that necroses and bleeds into the duodenum fits ampullary adenocarcinoma.

integration.text: The same few mechanisms recur along the whole tract. Chronic injury forces epithelium to keep proliferating, and either metaplasia (Barrett esophagus, intestinal metaplasia of the stomach) or regeneration (cirrhosis, inflamed colitis, inflamed bile ducts) gives mutations a dividing population in which to accumulate. Infection works through several routes: H. pylori through inflammation and antigen-driven B cell growth, HBV through integration, HPV-16 through E6 and E7 inactivation of p53 and Rb, and liver flukes through chronic ductal injury. Single-gene drivers explain other tumors: APC and mismatch repair genes in the colon, KRAS in the pancreas, CDH1 in diffuse gastric cancer, and KIT in GIST.

Anatomy and physiology then decide how a tumor shows itself. Lumen size and stool consistency separate right and left colon cancer; the course of the common bile duct through the pancreatic head explains painless jaundice; the thoracic duct explains the Virchow node; and portal drainage explains both why the liver is the commonest site of metastasis and why carcinoid syndrome waits for liver deposits. Markers such as AFP, CEA, CA 19-9, and urinary 5-HIAA reflect the biology of the tumor cell, but each has false positives and false negatives, so they support a diagnosis or track known disease rather than establish one alone.

summary: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma arises in the upper and middle third from alcohol, tobacco, and chronic mucosal injury; adenocarcinoma arises distally from reflux through Barrett esophagus.
Intestinal-type gastric cancer forms glands after H. pylori gastritis and intestinal metaplasia; diffuse type has signet ring cells, CDH1 loss, and linitis plastica.
Gastric MALT lymphoma depends on H. pylori-driven T cell help until t(11;18) makes it autonomous; GIST arises from KIT-mutant interstitial cells of Cajal.
Gastrinoma causes multiple and distal ulcers and steatorrhea from acid-inactivated lipase, with a paradoxical gastrin rise after secretin and a link to MEN1.
Carcinoid syndrome appears after liver metastases bypass hepatic MAO; lung MAO protects the left heart, so right-sided valves scar; urinary 5-HIAA is raised.
HBV and aflatoxin B1 (TP53 codon 249) can cause hepatocellular carcinoma directly; most other risks act through cirrhosis; AFP is raised and the tumor invades veins.
Metastases are the most common malignancy in the liver and peritoneum; hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor, and hepatocellular adenoma can rupture.
Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma (KRAS) causes painless jaundice with Courvoisier sign, plus migratory thrombophlebitis, weight loss, and raised CA 19-9.
Right colon cancer bleeds silently and causes iron deficiency anemia; left colon cancer constricts and obstructs; CEA tracks recurrence, not screening.
Adenoma risk rises with size, villous architecture, and dysplasia; sessile serrated lesions are premalignant through BRAF and methylation, unlike hyperplastic polyps.

verify: Percentages vary among sources and are given here as approximate: gastrinomas in MEN1 (about 20 to 25%), GIST by site (about 60% gastric, about 30% small intestine), pancreatic adenocarcinoma in the head (about 60%), KRAS mutation frequency (over 90%), and Warthin tumor bilaterality (about 10%).

The secretin stimulation test cutoff is quoted as a rise of 120 pg/mL or more in recent consensus and 200 pg/mL in older texts; the gastrin values in the worked example are illustrative, and fasting gastrin reference limits vary by assay.
The adult AFP reference limit (about 10 ng/mL) varies by laboratory; confirm whether NABNE expects a diagnostic threshold.

Whether gallbladder carcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma is called the most common biliary tract malignancy depends on whether intrahepatic tumors are counted; this chapter follows Robbins (gallbladder carcinoma for the extrahepatic biliary tract).
The term sessile serrated lesion has replaced sessile serrated adenoma or polyp in the current WHO classification; confirm which term NABNE uses.

Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Virchow node, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Krukenberg tumor, Trousseau syndrome, Courvoisier sign, Plummer-Vinson syndrome, Lauren classification, and Warthin tumor, or the descriptive terms as well.
The newer term metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease replaces nonalcoholic fatty liver disease; confirm which term NABNE uses.
